newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Poor hygiene kills 20 babies in Brazil hospital.
newsitem.headline: Poor hygiene kills 20 babies in Brazil hospital.

text.p: An infection caused by poor hygiene killed 20 babies in a maternity hospital in northern Brazil during 20 days in October, health minister Adib Jatene said on Wednesday.

Health officials were still trying to identify a strain of bacteria which killed the babies at Our Lady of Nazareth Hospital in the city of Boa Vista, near Brazil's border with Venezuela, Jatene told reporters.

Twelve other babies also died during the same period, but their deaths were attributed to "routine" causes -- mostly premature and complicated births. A further six infants were undergoing treatment for more common types of infection, he said.

An initial report into the tragedy showed staff at the hospital did not wash their hands before entering a post-natal intensive care ward, partly because sinks, soap and towels were scarce, and disinfection rules were not observed.

The report recommended the institution be kept open because 95 percent of hospital births in the Amazonian state of Roraima took place there. Experienced health officials had been sent to run the hospital and state attorneys would investigate the deaths.

"The problem was mostly down to hygiene," Jatene said. "When you have a big outbreak of infection in a hospital it is because hygiene standards were not met. We are trying now to find out why things went as far as they did."

Jatene said technical problems compounded the dismal situation in the hospital. Only four out of 15 incubators were working normally and power cuts left the city without power for up to 18 hours a day. No funds were available to buy a new generator, the minister said.

The tragedy in Boa Vista is the latest to beset Brazil's ailing health service. Nearly 100 elderly people were killed by a bacterial infection in a Rio de Janeiro clinic between April and July. Over 60 kidney dialysis patients in Caruaru, Pernambuco state, have died since March, believed to have been victims of contaminated water. Both clinics were private.
Jatene said "a large number" of Brazil's three million public and private sector health workers had little schooling and no training in nursing.
"We're in the process of reorganization but we can't eliminate all our deficiencies," the minister said. "That's the difference between a developed country and one that is still developing."
